newsitem.title: USA: N.Carolina bill seeks moratorium on big hog farms.
newsitem.headline: N.Carolina bill seeks moratorium on big hog farms.

text.p: A bill to halt construction of large hogs farms in North Carolina for one year was introduced in the state legislature on Tuesday.
The bill, introduced by Representative Richard Morgan, proposes a one-year moratorium on construction or expansion of any swine farm or waste lagoon in the state.

The move has the backing of North Carolina Governor Jim Hunt, who on April 9 proposed a two-year moratorium on expanding North Carolina's booming hog industry, which has grown rapidly in the 1990s to rank second after Iowa in total hog numbers.
"We must find a way to effectively and fairly zone for very large animal operations," Hunt said. "We must make sure zoning is done right, to protect our environment and to protect the farm economy."
As of March 1, North Carolina's hog herd totalled 8.45 million animals, second to Iowa's 10.8 million. In 1990, North Carolina's herd totalled 2.7 million hogs.

The state now has the nation's highest concentration of "mega" hog farms, defined as facilities with 2,000 or more hogs. That growth has also led to growing criticsm of hog farms' waste management, water pollution and odor problems.
Neither Morgan nor members of his staff were available for comment. A copy of the bill, H.B. 515, titled the Swine Farm Siting Act, was obtained by Reuters.

Along with the one-year moratorium, the bill would establish minimum distances between large hog operations and schools, parks, recreation areas, hospitals and homes, such as 1,500 feet from an occupied residence or 2,500 feet from parks or recreation areas.

The bill specifies public notice and hearings on construction plans for hog operations. It restricts location of waste lagoons away from floodplains, seeks new odor and licensing requirements, and proposes strict rules of review by state environmental and other agencies on hog operations.
It also allows neighboring property owners to file suit to seek injunctions and damages for violations of the act.
